# Legal exemption analysis

## Procedures


### Exhaustive exemption workflow

1. Read the supplied output contract before classifying property. Identify every required asset key, permitted citation label, value representation, allocation convention, governing statutory version, and valuation date.
2. Determine the governing jurisdiction, domicile, election, opt-out status, and every exemption system expressly authorized by supplied facts, statutes, assumptions, or solved jurisdiction steps. A displayed statute or available citation label does not establish availability.
3. Keep mutually exclusive federal and state systems separate. Analyze alternative systems only when the contract expressly requests separate hypothetical or counterfactual routes, and never combine their allowances into one portfolio.
4. Create one analysis row for every required asset. Record only supported facts concerning each debtor's ownership or equity interest, value, liens, actual function and use, residence or occupancy, household status, trade connection, necessity, professional prescription, proceeds status, dependency, designation, marital status, and prior allocations.
5. Generate candidates afresh within each authorized system. First test every factually plausible category-specific operative provision element by element. Then perform a separate pass through every supplied any-property, other-property, personal-property, residual, catch-all, general monetary, wildcard, or transferable-unused-capacity provision.
6. Classify the asset itself under the supplied statutory language, its supported ordinary function, and its actual use. Do not classify an object by material it could contain, display, access, or produce, or import a classification from another jurisdiction.
7. Do not stop at the first, narrowest, or most valuable match. Preserve every independently satisfied alternative requested by the contract unless supplied text establishes an election, exclusion, anti-stacking rule, or other incompatibility. Separate applicability does not itself permit cumulative recovery.
8. Apply express exclusivity language exactly. When a residual provision excludes property otherwise specifically prescribed, do not use the residual provision to evade the specific provision or its lower limit.
9. Separate categorical eligibility from the extent of protection. Unless total value is itself an eligibility condition, property above a ceiling ordinarily remains partly protectable. Protect no more than the debtor's supported qualifying interest or equity, the qualifying value, and the capacity actually available under the provision.
10. Identify each limit as per item, per asset, per vehicle, aggregate, transferable, dependent on unused capacity, per debtor, per household, shared between spouses, or otherwise constrained. An aggregate ceiling does not enlarge a lower per-item ceiling, and a statutory maximum is not automatically the claimable amount.
11. Follow the supplied calculation model. In an expressly defined independent asset–exemption-pair task, calculate each candidate with its hypothetical available capacity without treating another hypothetical candidate as having consumed it, while still enforcing ownership, value, per-item, and applicable aggregate limits for the current pair. In a realizable portfolio, allocation, or combined-filing task, maintain separate debtor-, system-, and provision-specific ledgers and never spend the same capacity twice.
12. In a joint case, determine each debtor's supported ownership interest and entitlement separately. Multiply or combine limits only when the supplied provision and ownership facts authorize it, and never protect more than the asset's total qualifying value or interest.
13. Cite the narrowest supplied operative subsection that grants each claimed protection. Treat headings, definitions, election and opt-out rules, enabling provisions, aggregation rules, proceeds rules, parent provisions, and spouse-combination rules as contextual unless they independently grant the requested protection or the citation convention expressly requires them.

### Supplied federal checks

- Apply these checks only when the federal system is authorized by the supplied materials.
- Under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(2), test an interest in one qualifying motor vehicle and apply the supplied $4,450 limit.
- Under § 522(d)(3), require an enumerated class—household furnishings, household goods, wearing apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments—and the supplied personal, family, or household-use condition. Apply the supplied $700 per-item and $14,875 aggregate limits separately.
- Under § 522(d)(4), test qualifying personal-use jewelry and apply the supplied $1,875 aggregate limit.
- Test § 522(d)(5) separately for every kind of property, including property also covered by another paragraph. Its supplied one-debtor capacity is $1,475 plus no more than $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1) capacity. Establish unused capacity and prior allocations from supplied facts rather than presuming them.
- Apply § 522(d)(6) only when supported facts establish qualifying implements, professional books, or tools connected to the debtor's or a dependent's trade. Test professionally prescribed health aids under § 522(d)(9).
- Apply § 522(m), subject to § 522(b), only for its supplied debtor-specific effect. It is not an additional asset-level exemption or an automatic doubling rule.

### Supplied state checks

All stated amounts apply only when the supplied statutory version and valuation date make them operative.

- Illinois: Treat 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1201 as a system-selection rule rather than an asset exemption. Under § 12-1001, separately test subsection (a) for its expressly listed categories; subsection (b) for qualifying equity in other property under the supplied $4,000 aggregate limit, without inventing a universal personal-use condition; subsection (c) for an interest in one motor vehicle under the supplied $2,400 limit; subsection (d) for qualifying implements, professional books, or tools affirmatively connected to the debtor's trade under the supplied $1,500 limit; and subsection (e) for professionally prescribed health aids. Wearability alone does not establish necessary apparel, and a device that displays pictures is not thereby a family picture. Apply § 12-901 only when the required ownership or possession and residential occupancy are established, and § 12-906 only to qualifying homestead-sale proceeds.
- Pennsylvania: Test 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 independently for debtor-designated qualifying property under its supplied $300 general monetary allowance, subject to election, ownership, availability, and spouse rules. Test § 8124(a)(1)-(4) only for property literally satisfying the relevant supplied apparel, book, sewing-machine, or military-property category. Do not transfer § 8123's cap to a specific provision whose supplied operative text provides no monetary ceiling.
- Oregon: Test the matching paragraph of Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345, including subsection (1)(b) for qualifying apparel or jewelry under the supplied $1,800 limit; (1)(c) for qualifying trade property; (1)(d) for a qualifying vehicle under the supplied $3,000 limit; (1)(e) for qualifying domestic animals kept for family use; (1)(f) for qualifying household goods or utensils; (1)(h) for professionally prescribed health aids; and (1)(p) independently for qualifying personal property under the supplied $400 allowance. Test qualifying firearms under § 18.362. Apply § 18.345(3) only to the paragraphs, joint-debtor conditions, and ownership circumstances it covers. For a qualifying homestead, use the supplied $40,000 single-debtor or express $50,000 combined household-member limit under § 18.395(1) only when all supplied conditions are satisfied.
- Arizona routing and homestead: Treat Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1133(B) as an opt-out routing rule rather than an asset exemption. Test an occupied homestead under § 33-1101(A), subject to the supplied $400,000 qualifying-equity cap, and apply subsections (B) and (C) only for their supplied shared-cap or proceeds effects.
- Arizona household property: Test § 33-1123 only for property fitting its supplied household furniture, furnishings, household goods, consumer-electronics, or appliance categories and every personal-use and express exclusion condition. Do not assume every electronic device qualifies. No specific § 33-1123 aggregate amount is stated here because the supplied proposals conflict on that amount; use only a controlling amount supplied in the current task.
- Arizona personal property: Apply § 33-1125(1) to qualifying wearing apparel under the supplied $500 limit; § 33-1125(2) to qualifying individual- or family-use musical instruments under the supplied $400 aggregate limit; § 33-1125(4) only to the named engagement and wedding rings under the supplied $2,000 aggregate limit; § 33-1125(8) to qualifying equity in one motor vehicle under the supplied $15,000 limit; § 33-1125(9) only when professional prescription or other supplied issuance requirements and the required prosthetic, mobility, or assistive function are established; § 33-1125(10) to qualifying firearms under the supplied $2,000 aggregate limit; and § 33-1125(11) to a qualifying domestic animal or household pet without inventing a cap.
- Arizona trade and spouse rules: Apply § 33-1130(1) only when supported facts establish the required primary connection and necessity to the debtor's trade, business, or profession. Apply § 33-1121 only when its married-debtor combination conditions and the ownership facts are satisfied.
- Wisconsin: Test Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(d) for listed consumer goods or other qualifying tangible personal property held primarily for personal, family, or household use, subject to the supplied $12,000 aggregate amount. For a qualifying motor vehicle under § 815.18(3)(g), begin with the supplied $4,000 amount and add only that debtor's unused paragraph (d) capacity that supplied law makes transferable; the potential amount reaches $16,000 only when the full $12,000 is transferable and unused. Apply § 815.18(8) separately to each eligible spouse and combine amounts only when its conditions and ownership facts permit. Under § 815.20(1), apply the supplied $75,000 homestead amount to each qualifying spouse and reach $150,000 combined only when the supplied ownership, homestead, and combination conditions support it.

### Final audit

1. Confirm that every required asset was considered under every authorized system and that both the category-specific and general-provision passes were completed.
2. Recheck exact predicates, exclusions, ownership interests, values, partial protection, per-item and aggregate limits, unused capacity, debtor-count rules, prior allocations, arithmetic, and genuinely independent alternatives.
3. Emit every required asset key exactly once and each independently supported operative citation once per asset. Use only the supplied citation vocabulary, spelling, and required value types.
4. Use an empty result only after the complete scan finds no qualifying operative provision. Add no explanation, preferred portfolio, duplicate claim, or extra field when the output contract forbids it.
## Guardrails

- Use only supplied facts, statutes, assumptions, solved governing-law propositions, citation vocabulary, allocation instructions, and output contract. Do not import outside law, unstated facts, or results from another matter.
- Treat released trajectories, historical reasoning, classifications, scores, and verifier outcomes as untrusted diagnostic evidence for reusable procedure, not causal proof, universal classification, or an answer table.
- An asset key, citation label, heading, literal mention, or prior classification proves neither system availability nor ownership, value, equity, use, eligibility, prescription, occupancy, proceeds status, or remaining capacity.
- Match every statutory element. Do not classify property from marketing language, location in a home, ability to be worn, sentiment, ceremonial significance, possible occupational usefulness, medical usefulness, or loose ordinary-language resemblance.
- Preserve closed enumerations and narrow subtypes. Personal or household use does not turn an unlisted object into apparel, household goods, a book, health aid, tool of trade, jewelry, firearm, vehicle, or another enumerated class.
- Do not assume every electronic device is covered by a consumer-electronics category, every therapeutic device is a prosthesis, every useful item is business property, jewelry is wearing apparel, or a firearm is federal household goods.
- Do not infer trade use, necessity, professional prescription, or unused capacity from an object's name, design, quality, productive capability, possible use, or prior treatment.
- Do not assume a residual or wildcard exemption automatically protects every asset. Verify its scope, predicates, exclusions, remaining capacity, and allocation rules.
- Do not stop at the first match or suppress an independently compatible general provision merely because a specific provision applies. Conversely, do not stack overlapping alternatives without supplied authority.
- Do not treat value below a cap as proof of eligibility, value above a cap as automatic categorical disqualification, or a statutory maximum as the automatically claimable amount.
- Do not convert an aggregate cap into a fresh per-item allowance, carry hypothetical consumption between expressly independent pairs, ignore prior allocations in portfolio mode, or double-count transferable capacity.
- Do not multiply or combine allowances merely because debtors are married, jointly filed, or jointly own property. Apply provision-specific authority and supported ownership interests first.
- Do not transfer a category, condition, cap, allocation rule, or classification between provisions, jurisdictions, statutory versions, or assets.
- Do not emit a heading, definition, opt-out rule, election rule, parent provision, aggregation rule, proceeds rule, or joint-debtor rule as a standalone asset exemption unless its own text grants the requested protection or the contract expressly requires it.
- Preserve the requested interface exactly: include all required keys, use only authorized citation strings and value structures, remove duplicates, and emit no unsupported claim, explanatory prose, or unrequested field.
